A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TIED research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–C are readable and support matching retained content across renumbering, relocation and additions.

before.justification: V1 reports original SO(10) sampling experiments, transformed-MNIST classification and FID results, and heat/Burgers PDE experiments, with additional statistical and runtime results in Appendix C.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds affNIST compute-budget and noise-schedule studies, plus image-inversion examples.

M1.justification: The posterior formulation, diffusion process, Monte Carlo score estimator and Algorithm 1 updates are retained. Section B.10 newly documents lowest-energy sample selection and omission of the data-action Jacobian term; it does not establish that these implementation practices changed between versions.

E1.justification: Both versions cover SO(10) synthetic sampling, affine/homography-transformed MNIST, and heat/Burgers PDEs, including augmented heat-equation training. The added analyses use existing affNIST coverage rather than introducing another dataset, task or transformation scenario.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged within corresponding experiments: kinetic Langevin for synthetic sampling; ITS, FoCal, kinetic Langevin and LieLAC for applicable image comparisons; and FoCal, kinetic Langevin and LieLAC for PDEs. V2's Table 1 shortens kinetic Langevin to Langevin; affConv/homConv reference results remain.

E3.justification: New affNIST experiments vary score-estimation sample count N across 1, 2, 5 and 10, diffusion steps M across 10, 20, 50 and 100, and seven noise schedules including constant-noise controls. Existing benchmark splits, metrics and Table 3 configurations remain unchanged. Newly disclosed ensemble and ITS settings do not establish revisions to earlier experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds systematic compute-versus-accuracy analysis and noise-schedule sensitivity/ablation experiments, including controls testing the importance of annealing (Tables 6–7). New image-correction and comparative inversion examples (Figures 4 and 7–11) also expand case-study evidence. These substantially broaden analysis beyond v1's benchmark demonstrations.

E5.justification: V2 carries existing accuracy error bars from v1's Appendix Table 4 into Table 1 and specifies five seeds, resolving v1's conflicting three-test prose and five-test caption. However, the explicit identification of the spread as standard deviation disappears. Neither additional runs nor new statistical tests are established.

E6.justification: V2 reconciles Table 1 and Section 5.2's affine/classifier accuracy from 85.64% to 82.64%, already reported in v1's Appendix Table 4; this is not evidence of a performance decline. New Tables 6–7 report accuracies spanning 75.45–83.78% across compute settings and 60.00%/59.80% for constant-noise controls. Image examples are added; other matched benchmark scores and runtime values remain unchanged.

T1.justification: New Proposition B.9 proves that selecting the maximum-likelihood element among independent samples preserves equivariance, assuming an almost-surely unique maximizer. This is a bounded theoretical addition; the existing posterior, reverse-diffusion, target-score and consistency proofs remain substantively intact.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: probabilistic transformation inversion on general Lie groups, a trivialized diffusion sampler, test-time equivariance and improved image/PDE robustness. Additional evidence and the corrected accuracy do not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Section B.1 newly discusses non-free actions, stabilizer redundancy and potentially non-normalizable posteriors, while arguing that practical recovery remains possible. Appendix C adds interpretations of compute tradeoffs and constant-noise failures, and Section 5.2 emphasizes classifier self-correction. Existing explanations of benchmark behavior are retained.

D1.justification: Section B.10 discloses crucial previously undocumented inference choices: selecting the lowest-energy sample among K=64 draws, matching LieLAC initializations, including ensemble cost in comparisons, and dropping the data-action Jacobian term. Appendix C also specifies eight ITS search levels. These materially improve implementation reproducibility; existing hardware, sampler configurations and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: Section 4.2 adds Milnor (1976) and explains which practical groups fall outside bi-invariant-metric assumptions, sharpening the existing comparison with earlier target-score work. The broader related-work positioning is retained; most other reference changes concern publication or bibliographic metadata.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized language corrections, adds proof sketches and explanatory algorithm comments, introduces Section B.10, and organizes Appendix C into named discussions. Conference information and acknowledgments also change. The overall narrative and section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds an image-correction figure, a forward-diffusion illustration, comparative image galleries and two analysis tables. It also merges the appendix accuracy/error-bar display into Table 1, reformats Algorithm 1 with comments, and relocates retained displays. These substantially expand visual explanation and evidence beyond ordinary reflow or renumbering.

improvement.justification: V2 improves transparency and support by reconciling the conflicting accuracy reports, documenting important inference choices, proving selection equivariance and adding useful compute/noise sensitivity evidence. These strengthen an otherwise largely retained paper. The gains remain bounded: the new ablations concern one existing setting, and the claimed negligible effect of omitting the Jacobian lacks a dedicated comparison.
